Original: It’s the mornings after the spider-and-heights dreams that are the most painful, that it takes sometimes three coffees and two showers and sometimes a run to loosen the grip on his soul’s throat; and these post-dream mornings are even worse if he wakes unalone, if the previous night’s Subject is still there, wanting to twitter, or to cuddle and, like, spoon, asking what exactly is the story with the foggy inverted tumblers on the bathroom floor, commenting on his night-sweats, clattering around in the kitchen, making kippers or bacon or something more hideous and unhoneyed he’s supposed to eat with post-coital male gusto, the ones who have this thing about they call it Feeding My Man, wanting a man who can barely keep down A.M. honey-toast to east with male gusto, elbows out and sovelling, making little noises. Even when alone, unable to uncurl alone and sit slowly up and wing out the sheet and go to the bathroom, these darkest mornings start days that Orin can’t even bring himself for hours to think about how he’ll get through the day. These worst mornings with cold floors and hot windows and merciless light — the soul’s certainty that the day will have to be not traversed but sort of climbed, vertically, and then that going to sleep again at the end of it will be like falling, again, off something tall and sheer.
Paragraph1: Orin’s mornings often began as a kind of existential residue, the aftermath of dreams that seemed to gnaw their way out from the deep recesses of the psyche’s cellar, dreams that were equal parts spiders and sheer verticality, both suffocating and vertiginous. The mornings required ritual, regimented almost to the point of ceremony: coffee brewed to a darkness that could rival the void, showers so scalding they left his skin reddened, runs that turned his lungs into bellows just to remind himself he was alive. Yet the presence of a Subject—the capital "S" both deliberate and derisive, a holdover from what Orin thought of as his internal marketing manual for coping with emotional distance—would complicate the sequence. Subjects had a tendency toward earnest, unbidden gestures: talking as though morning were a shared phenomenon, attempting to wrap him in the tangled warmth of their limbs, even cooking eggs with a kind of oblivious cheer that Orin could only describe as offensive. The worst was the silence, the gap in conversation where their gaze hung too long on him, expectant. Alone, though, wasn’t better. The walls of his apartment took on the sheen of inevitability, the day ahead a Sisyphean incline of meetings and errands and human interactions that he already knew would leave him feeling as drained as the coffee grounds spiraling down his sink. This, he thought, was life’s greatest irony: that waking up alive could feel so much like falling.
Paragraph2: Meanwhile, Orin’s nocturnally tormented with disturbing nightmares, dreams of falling through endless black space from great heights, or being chased by human-sized spiders, or sometimes both, dreams of enormous spiders pursuing him to a rooftop’s edge, from which he awakes totally emotionally drained and suffocated and physically drenched in sweat. Orin’s constructed a number of morning rituals to mitigate the queasy, sucked-out feeling his dreams give him, which rituals have grown more repetitive and elongated with time, such that he now needs to drink multiple cups of coffee, have two or sometimes three showers, and go on a run before he feels even remotely normal. On those mornings when he has a Subject still in his bed from the night before, and therefore for obvious reasons can’t indulge his full routine, he finds himself privately ruminating on his disturbing and repetitive nightmares while he and the Subject are cuddling, chatting or cooking breakfast together, all while she remains totally oblivious to his tormented internal state. So that paradoxically, waking up next to a partner actually makes him feel even greater discomfort and alienation than if he were alone. Though make no mistake, mornings alone are almost unbearably oppressive, even the routines do little to alleviate Orin’s dread of the day ahead, the coming day seeming to him alternately like an insurmountable vertical climb or yet another fall from a great height.

Original: That was all. I knew then that if Margaret got me kicked out, it wouldn’t be for doing a thing as normal as sleeping with my master. And somehow, that disturbed me. I felt almost as though I really was doing something shameful, happily playing whore for my supposed owner. I went away feeling uncomfortable, vaguely ashamed.Time passed. Kevin and I became more a part of the household, familiar, accepted, accepting. That disturbed me too when I thought about it. How easily we seemed to acclimatize. Not that I wanted us to have trouble, but it seemed as though we should have had a harder time adjusting to this particular segment of history—adjusting to our places in the household of a slaveholder. For me, the work could be hard, but was usually more boring than physically wearing. And Kevin complained of boredom, and of having to be sociable with a steady stream of ignorant pretentious guests who visited the Weylin house. But for drop-ins from another century, I thought we had had a remarkably easy time. And I was perverse enough to be bothered by the ease.“This could be a great time to live in.”Kevin said once. “I keep thinking what an experience it would be to stay in it—go West and watch the building of the country, see how much of the Old West mythology is true.”“West,” I said bitterly. “That’s where they’re doing it to the Indians instead of the blacks!”
Paragraph1: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger. She could get me whipped, or kicked out. Not for something as normal as sleeping with one's master - there were already slaves who were forced to do that. No, my transgressions would be more subtle - and so I would have to be on closer guard. I made a note to speak to Kevin about this. In the weeks we had been at the house, I'd notice how we'd both adjusted to our new life. I did the work of a slave with the same attitude I had done my chores as a child. Endless drudgery. Bowed heads when the white folks passed. And then dinner out back and a dreamless sleep on the floor. Meanwhile Kevin spent his days in the library; asking Tom questions about how to get out West. "Maybe we could escape, to California," Kevin had said, a few nights ago. "California's a thousand miles away," I said, shaking my head. "Even if we could forge convincing freedom papers, we'd probably die of dengue fever along the way." I didn't add the other thing I was thinking - that it wouldn't be any better out West, where Native Americans were being slaughtered. I couldn't stand to see Kevin get that mystified look on his face. The longer we remained in the house, the more aware I became of our differences.
Paragraph2: I sat in the corner of the room, watching Kevin's face light up as he talked about exploring the West, and felt the familiar twist of unease in my stomach. The shame wasn't sharp anymore – that's what frightened me most. We had learned to live here, learned to accept the unacceptable with a casualness that made my skin crawl when I let myself think about it. The work wasn't what haunted me; it was the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes until they started to feel like your own. Margaret's presence loomed over us, not because she might seduce our master – that would have been too simple, too normal – but because she represented everything we were becoming: adaptable, compliant, surviving. Kevin didn't see it that way. His eyes held that historian's gleam, that detached fascination with a time he saw as a story to be witnessed. "Think of seeing the Old West firsthand," he said, and I had to bite back bitter laughter. I wanted to shake him, make him understand that while black bodies were being broken in these Southern fields, native peoples were being slaughtered in his romantic frontier. There was no safe place to stand and observe, no neutral ground from which to watch history unfold. We were in it, drowning in it, and our very ability to adapt was becoming our curse.

Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.
Paragraph1: The winter light was dimming, Saint Patrick’s Day fading into a muted gray.  I sat beside her bed, the green Jell-O untouched on the bedside table, a festive offering she couldn’t partake in.  Outside, the snow was falling, the last of winter’s icy grip, the sunlight reflecting off the white expanse in a dazzling display.  But in this room, there was a different kind of dimming, a slow, inevitable burning down to smoke.She wasn’t asleep, not quite, but somewhere between here and there, her breath shallow, her body still.  Yet, her eyes, those strikingly blue eyes, remained open, vivid against the pale skin, the stark white sheets.  It was in those eyes that I saw it all unfold – the bitterness that had clung to her like a shroud, the bewilderment at the body’s betrayal, and then, finally, a quiet heroism.  The blue, so vibrant, so alive, was a defiance, a refusal to let go, even as the current pulled her away.I watched her, my mother, her spirit flickering like a candle flame in the gathering darkness.  And in those blue depths, I saw the echo of the life she had lived, the love she had given, the strength she had shown.  It was a story written in the language of the heart, a story that would live on, even as the last embers of her life faded away.
Paragraph2: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.

Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.
Paragraph1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
Paragraph2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

Original: "The only reason you say that race was not an issue is because you wish it was not. We all wish it was not. But it’s a lie. I came from a country where race was not an issue; I did not think of myself as black and I only became black when I came to America. When you are black in America and you fall in love with a white person, race doesn’t matter when you’re alone together because it’s just you and your love. But the minute you step outside, race matters. But we don’t talk about it. We don’t even tell our white partners the small things that piss us off and the things we wish they understood better, because we’re worried they will say we’re overreacting, or we’re being too sensitive. And we don’t want them to say, Look how far we’ve come, just forty years ago it would have been illegal for us to even be a couple blah blah blah, because you know what we’re thinking when they say that? We’re thinking why the fuck should it ever have been illegal anyway? But we don’t say any of this stuff. We let it pile up inside our heads and when we come to nice liberal dinners like this, we say that race doesn’t matter because that’s what we’re supposed to say, to keep our nice liberal friends comfortable. It’s true. I speak from experience." The host, a Frenchwoman, glanced at her American husband, a slyly pleased smile on her face; the most unforgettable dinner parties happened when guests said unexpected, and potentially offensive, things.The poet shook her head and said to the host, “I’d love to take some of that wonderful dip home if you have any left,” and looked at the others as though she could not believe they were actually listening to Ifemelu. But they were, all of them hushed, their eyes on Ifemelu as though she was about to give up a salacious secret that would both titillate and implicate them. Ifemelu had been drinking too much white wine; from time to time she had a swimming sensation in her head, and she would later send apology e-mails to the host and the poet. But everyone was watching her, even Blaine, whose expression she could not, for once, read clearly. And so she began to talk about Curt.
Paragraph1: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."
Paragraph2: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."

Original: It was early winter, the first frost of the year. My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors. Fumbling in her sewing box, she found some white cloth that would do for a newborn’s gown. Gripped by contractions and terribly afraid, tears started down as she plied her needle. She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.
Paragraph1: The dawn light, a brutal white gash in the belly of the night, illuminated her blood-soaked hands, the scissors glinting ominously.  The air, thick with the metallic scent of life and death, echoed her ragged breaths, each one a desperate prayer.  She had become a primal vessel, fear and pain etching lines on her face, a grotesque map of motherhood.  The room, a battlefield of sweat and tears, cradled the echo of her final push, the newborn’s slippery form a dark miracle against the faded floorboards.  With trembling hands, she severed the cord, the last physical tie to a world that seemed to have abandoned her.Her voice, hoarse and raw, filled the silence, a chant for life, a plea to whatever gods might be listening.  But the newborn’s cry, a fleeting spark in the vast emptiness, was swallowed by the shadows.  The silence returned, heavier now, crushing her with its finality.  She clutched the lifeless body to her breast, her warmth a futile offering to the cold stillness that had settled over them.  The world outside continued its relentless march, oblivious to the silent tragedy unfolding within those walls.  The floor, cold and unforgiving, seeped into her bones, mirroring the icy grip of grief that threatened to consume her.
Paragraph2: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.

Original: I am failing as a woman. I am failing as a feminist. To freely accept the feminist label would not be fair to good feminists. If I am, indeed, a feminist, I am a rather bad one. I am a mess of contradictions. There are many ways in which I am doing feminism wrong, at least according to the way my perceptions of feminism have been warped by being a woman.I want to be independent, but I want to be taken care of and have someone to come home to. I have a job I’m pretty good at. I am in charge of things. I am on committees. People respect me and take my counsel. I want to be strong and professional, but I resent how hard I have to work to be taken seriously, to receive a fraction of the consideration I might otherwise receive. Sometimes I feel an overwhelming need to cry at work, so I close my office door and lose it. I want to be in charge and respected and in control, but I want to surrender, completely, in certain aspects of my life. Who wants to grow up? When I drive to work, I listen to thuggish rap at a very loud volume even though the lyrics are degrading to women and offend me to my core. The classic Ying Yang Twins song “Salt Shaker”? It’s amazing. “Bitch you gotta shake it till your camel starts to hurt.”Poetry.(I am mortified by my music choices.)I care what people think.Pink is my favorite color. I used to say my favorite color was black to be cool, but it is pink—all shades of pink. If I have an accessory, it is probably pink. I read Vogue, and I’m not doing it ironically, though it might seem that way. I once live-tweeted the September issue. I demonstrate little outward evidence of this, but I have a very indulgent fantasy where I have a closet full of pretty shoes and purses and matching outfits. I love dresses. For years I pretended I hated them, but I don’t. Maxi dresses are one of the finest clothing items to become popular in recent memory. I have opinions on maxi dresses! I shave my legs! Again, this mortifies me. If I take issue with the unrealistic standards of beauty women are held to, I shouldn’t have a secret fondness for fashion and smooth calves, right?
Paragraph1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.
Paragraph2: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.
Paragraph1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling my close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
Paragraph2: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. In the quiet of our Istanbul apartment, the weight of the manuscript in my hands mirrored the gravity of the step I was about to take. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. My father, however, had always encouraged the flickering flame of my aspirations. He took the manuscript with an easy, almost playful smile, as though we were conspirators in some artistic rebellion. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. He didn’t speak immediately; instead, he held me, his silence filled with a fatherly pride that words might have diminished. Then, in a voice steadied by conviction, he said I would succeed and even prophesied a prestigious prize in my future. The precision of his faith startled me—how could he be so sure when I wasn’t? This memory, so vivid and immutable, grew to anchor me, particularly after his death in 2002. It is strange how the weight of approval from someone who is no longer there can linger like a ghost in the room, shaping the contours of your own self-belief. My father’s prediction, his prophecy of my future success, stands as a monument to his faith in me, a beacon amidst the ever-shifting uncertainties of life and art.

Original: The road went on through a shadeless burn and for miles there were only the charred shapes of trees in a dead land where nothing moved save windy rifts of ash that rose dolorous and died again down the blackened corridors.Late in the day the road brought him into a swamp. And that was all. Before him stretched a spectral waste out of which reared only the naked trees in attitudes of agony and dimly hominoid like figures in a landscape of the damned. A faintly smoking garden of the dead that tended away to the earth’s curve. He tried his foot in the mire before him and it rose in a vulvate welt claggy and sucking. He stepped back. A stale wind blew from this desolation and the marsh reeds and black ferns among which he stood clashed softly like things chained. He wondered why a road should come to such a place.Going back the way by which he came he met again the blind man tapping through the dusk. He waited very still by the side of the road, but the blind man passing turned his head and smiled upon him his blind smile. Holme watched him out of sight. He wondered where the blind man was going and did he know how the road ended. Someone should tell a blind man before setting him out that way.
Paragraph1: The road stretched out before Holme like a wound in the earth, ash drifting across its surface in spectral waves that moved without wind. The charred and twisted trees rose up from the swampland like ancient mariners frozen in their death throes, their blackened limbs reaching toward a colorless sky that held neither sun nor promise. He tested the mire with one boot and watched the earth shudder and contract like something alive yet unborn, the surface dimpling and rising again in slow persistent waves that spoke of depths best left unplumbed. Through the dead forest came a sound like bones rattling, though there was nothing there but naked branches clicking together in a wind that seemed to carry voices. Then came the blind man, tapping his way along the road's edge with a stick worn smooth as glass, his face lifted in permanent expectation, smiling as if he knew some secret that the seeing world had lost. Holme watched him pass, this prophet of the wastes, and thought how the man's blindness might be a mercy in such a place as this. For what use were eyes in a world become nothing but ash and shadow, where even the trees had forgotten their own names and stood like sentinels at the gates of some darker realm that lay just beyond the next bend in the road, waiting with infinite patience for travelers who would never return.
Paragraph2: Holme kept to the road that wound long into a landscape of ash and cinder, charred trees skeletal in their moorings of roots twisting up through a hellscape of the dead. He walked on. Further on he came to a swamp that fell nightmarish on his eyes in all its nakedness of trees and dark figures dimly hominoid seemingly skulking in the mire. With a wary toe he tested the swampwater and reeled backwards at its unsure footing of bog and moss, crags of rock wet against the backdrop of windcurrents clashing the sodden vegetation and his feeling of desolation. He would not go this way. Retracing his steps back to the road and setting out upon it again he soon saw a man up ahead. The man tapped and swept a walking stick before him, feeling his way through that forever darkness only the blind knew the language of. The man smiled at Holme as he passed. Where the blind man was going Holme had already been, and Holme wondered then if anyone had informed the man of the grimness of what lay ahead at the end of the road. Walking on he lingered on what was not lost on him, the blind man’s incapability of seeing the burnt-out trees or even the road before him, not ever knowing where he’s going, but still following the road. No, he thought. He didn’t know where he was going.

Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.
Paragraph1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
Paragraph2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.
